name: The Osborn household — a name from the post office's letter lists
head: osborn_wm

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of March 1835 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1835-05-20, 50 days later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1835-03-31 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

arrival_year.note: THE MAN'S OWN RECOLLECTION, NOT A CONTEMPORARY RECORD. He registered at the Calumet Club on the roll of 1879 and gave 1834, May 1, as his date of coming to Chicago — forty-four years after the fact. The roll's own `arrival_year_basis` says it dates the claim and does not prove it, so the year is carried at `inferred` and the household's `arrival` block keeps the bound the contemporary evidence sets.

origin.note: A BIRTHPLACE, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME CLAIM. The Calumet Club roll of 1879 gives “Ridgefield, Conn.” as where this man was BORN; this field asks where the household came FROM, and a generation that moved west in stages frequently did not come from the state it was born in. It is carried as the best statement of origin the sources make about this household and not as a last residence.

reason_for_coming.value: The 1834 season: the harbour works, the opening of the bar and the trade that followed them
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THE SEASON AND NOTHING ELSE. No trade is recorded for this household and no source says why it came; the only thing the evidence gives is when it was here by. This states the draws that were operating in that season and chooses among them nowhere. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says why this household came, or a committed source that apportions the town's arrivals between the land sales, the canal and the harbour works

persons.name: Wm. Osborn

later_occupation.note: NONE RECORDED FOR 1835 — AND A TRADE IS RECORDED FOR 1839. This is a POINTER at `directories.people[].occupation_later` on this same record, derived by `tools/qualify_later_trades.py` and holding nothing that block does not already say. It is not a claim about the scene date: the 1835 occupation above still reads `none_recorded`, its grade has not moved, and no premises has been sought on the strength of it, because a directory of 1839 is evidence about 1839. It is written because the field a reader consults was asserting an absence this file contradicts three lines further down, and "no trade anywhere" and "no trade in the scene window, one printed 1839" are not the same fact (T-0693).

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. A list of uncalled-for letters prints a name and no trade, and this pass will not read one in.

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Osbern, Wm.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Osborn, William, | 1834, May 1, | Ridgefield, Conn. | 67 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'william' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json).

resident_research.summary: Will County history places a William Osborn among Thorn Creek settlers in 1833-34. This is geographically plausible for a Chicago post-office contact, but the common name and Will County residence are insufficient for a merge.

conflicts: Will County geography and common name; no direct Chicago bridge.

roles.note: A TRADE PRINTED AGAINST THIS NAME IN A LATER VOLUME, and this row says which year rather than leaving it to a pointer (T-0693, carried here by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). `role` is null because the directory's wording has not been adjudicated into the closed vocabulary — the printing is what the source gives and the printing is what is kept. T-1254 is where the controlled term is ruled on. It is not a claim about 1835-07-01 and never becomes one: the year is 1839.

A TRADE PRINTED IN THE 1843 DIRECTORY, 8 years after the scene, carried here by its crosswalk (T-1254, by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). It is NOT a claim about 1835-07-01 and never becomes one: back-projecting a later volume onto the scene is the defect T-1145 exists to refuse. `place` is the address or place of business the record states in its own column; a firm named only inside the printed line stays in `as_printed` for the business band to rule on.

age_band.note: THE BAND THIS PERSON'S OWN BIRTH YEAR PUTS THEM IN on 1 July 1835. It is a view of a value already on this card and adds nothing to it; it exists so the age axis can be read across the whole layer at once, beside the bands the model draws for everybody else.

sex_basis.note: 'Wm.' IS THE PERIOD CONTRACTION OF William, and every expansion of it attested in this project is a man's name — so the contraction settles the sex without settling which name was contracted. The table is data/research/residents/forename_sex.json.

birth_year.note: A BIRTH INTERVAL OUT OF A MAN'S OWN STATEMENT OF HIS AGE. He registered at the Calumet Club's reception to the settlers of Chicago on 27 May 1879 and gave his age as 67: "Osborn, William, | 1834, May 1, | Ridgefield, Conn. | 67 | Chicago.". An age of 67 completed years given on that day means the birth falls after 27 May 1811 and on or before 27 May 1812, so the birth year is 1811 or 1812. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth. IT IS A RECOLLECTION, forty-four years after the scene date — better than a recollection about somebody else, and still not a record. The merge onto this person is the old-settler crosswalk's own (OS2A), in data/research/old_settlers/people.json.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

surname_collision.note: A COLLISION SAID, NOT ACTED ON. Run against the tree as it stands, this pass would not MINT this card: refusal 8 — 'surname already minted' — lands on it, because B. Osborn already holds the family name Osborn. The owner ruled on 2026-09-18 (T-0660, option (c)) that refusals 7 and 8 are MINT-TIME rules: they decide whether a new household may be minted on a family name the town already spends, and they do not un-mint one that already stands. So this record is not retired, its id is not redirected at anybody, the town's population does not move, and the research row and directory matches it carries are not stranded on a retirement nothing draws. What has changed is that the collision is legible: a reader sees both cards and why both are here. REFUSAL 8 IS NOT A CLAIM THAT TWO RECORDS ARE ONE PERSON — it is a limit on how much one pass may assert on a family name. Two of the collisions this reading uncovered are two different men. The pass's `rank()` is unchanged and the cohort is not re-derived; that was option (b)'s cost and the ruling declined to pay it. The derivation behind this block, both readings side by side, is docs/RESEARCH/letter-list-surname-collisions.md.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. osborn_wm, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1119 (a single entry); osborn_wm, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e1934 (a single entry).

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Osborn, William, boot, shoe, and leather merchant, 141 Lake st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. The 1835 record prints no trade for this person, so there is no 1835 business for a later door to position. Minting one out of a directory printed after the scene date is the one thing this pass may never do. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause 1).
